title: Your study rule
hookLine: one page for study: Benedict's Rule set hours for reading, a book for Lent, and seniors who walked the halls
tomorrow: a saint wrote of a dark night. was the dark a sign to quit?

lines: SENIORS WHO GO AROUND AND CHECK.
cards: Some libraries have a person who quietly walks the study room. So did one monastery rule. The Rule of Saint Benedict, written for monks, sets hours for reading every day.
Then comes a strange instruction. At reading time, one or two senior monks are to go around the monastery and check. Not for stolen books.
For a monk who is idle, or chatting, and keeping the others from reading. Why would a holy rule need hall monitors?

teach.h: IDLENESS IS THE ENEMY OF THE SOUL.
teach.b: Because the Rule doesn't trust reading to take care of itself. The chapter opens with a line usually translated: idleness is the enemy of the soul. So the Rule doesn't leave study to mood.
It fixes the day: hours for work with the hands, hours for reading.

teach.h: ONE BOOK, READ ALL THE WAY THROUGH.
teach.b: And in Lent, it says, each monk receives a book from the library and reads it through, from beginning to end. Not sampling. One book, all the way.

teach.h: LECTIO: SLOW READING AT SET TIMES.
teach.b: That's the Benedictine practice called lectio, sacred reading: slow, at set times, with the book given rather than picked by whim. And the rounds weren't about slow readers.

They looked for the idle one who distracts others. The same chapter says a brother who can't study should be given work instead, so he isn't idle, and the weak get work light enough that they aren't crushed by it.
The rule fits the person. Here's the teaching for a rule of your own. Study, the Benedictine way, isn't a burst of inspiration.

teach.h: A TIME, A BOOK, SOMEONE WHO NOTICES.
teach.b: It's three plain things: a time, a book, and someone or something that notices when you drift.
All three fit on one page.

how: Benedictine monks keep set hours for lectio, slow sacred reading, and the Rule assigns each monk a book to read through in Lent. On a personal rule, study is usually one book, a set time, and someone who checks in.

o: a promise to read every book you buy within a month
a strict class schedule handed down by a teacher
a time, one book, and someone who notices, on one page

games.q: Benedict's reading hours: tap the pairs.
p: one book from the library, read through
go around at reading time and check
slow sacred reading at set times

s: Benedict left reading to each monk's mood
he fixed hours for reading every day, alongside hours of work.
a monk who couldn't study was given other work instead
so he wasn't idle. the rule fits the person.
the seniors walked around to punish slow readers
they looked for anyone idle or chatting and keeping others from reading.

games.q: your book club picks a long book. three weeks in, you're dipping into random chapters. what would Benedict's Lent rule say?
o: read it through, beginning to end, at a set time.
skim the best chapters; the point is the ideas.
swap it for something shorter that grabs you more.
games.why: in Lent each monk got one book from the library and read it through, start to finish. not sampling.

practice: Write your study rule in three lines: when you'll read, which one book you'll read through, and who or what will notice if you drift. Keep it to what fits on one page. Then sit with the page in front of you until the bell.

wordCard.voice: Your study rule: a time, one book, and someone who notices, written down, the way Benedict ordered the reading hours.

orig.note: Latin: reading. Benedictines speak of lectio, slow sacred reading.

carryVoice: Your line: study. Benedict gave each monk one book and the hours to read it. Day 1668, and the study stretch is complete.

sources.ref: Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 48 (idleness the enemy of the soul; hours of work and reading; a book from the library in Lent, read through; seniors go round at reading time; other work for those who cannot read)
